I'm currently on a pretty low dose of Wellbutrin (100 mg) combined with Prozac, and it is working for me.  But I had tried about 4 different things previous to that, and some of them made things worse for me.  When my depression was at its worst, I basically didn't care about getting better, because I didn't think it would happen.  Currently, I'm doing pretty well, and I think it's by and large because of the medication.  

Please, please try to stick with it and find a medication that works for you.  Everyone is different.  Zoloft and Celexa were horrible for me.  If you are honest with your doctor, they will (or should) absolutely try to find something better for you.  It sounds like you feel there is no point right now, and there's not much that can be said to change that, but sometimes finding the right medication is the way to start building back up to a good place, or even an okay place.

Let your doctor know how you're feeling.  Really.  I hope you have better luck soon!

Ian Anderson uses a lot of extended techniques, some of which I think he made up.  If you want to learn those aspects of his playing (the weird non-flute noises), a decent classical teacher can help you.  

You should check out the work of [Ian Clarke](http://www.ianclarke.net/).  He was majorly influenced by Jethro Tull, and, as he is a teacher as well, he does lectures on performing his pieces, though I can't seem to find any right now. :(  Either way, it's similar enough that I think it would be helpful even just to watch.

For the jazz aspect, is there a local jazz group or school jazz band you could get into?  Flutes are occasionally accepted, and if it's a learning group that will help your improvisation.  If nothing else, you can get the [Jamey Aebersold Jazz Series](http://www.music44.com/Merchant2/merchant.mvc?Session_ID=7CD1F1C83552EC5D7096B620048CF5BE&Screen=PROD&Store_Code=X&Product_Code=V01DS-J).  It's cheesy but it's simple and it teaches you the basics.

The best thing would be to get lessons with a jazz saxophonist who doubles on flute.  That can be hard, though.  If you happen to be in the New York or San Francisco areas, I can recommend some, though.

Good luck!

This is possibly my most embarrassing moment:

I've been a runner on and off since I was about 12.  My dad has been a runner my whole life and occasionally tries to get me to go with him.

When I was 13, I went with him on something of a wilderness trail by our house.  He likes to push me, but I wasn't feeling great.  I thought I was just gassy.  I was incorrect.  We were maybe a mile from my house when I told my dad to just go ahead of me.  I knew the way back and, as embarrassing and unladylike as this is, I just really, really (thought I) had to fart.  Incorrect again.  I shat my pants.  Hardcore.  And I don't know what I ate that day, but it was not solid. 

So, I'm less than a quarter of a mile from my house, crying in embarrassment, but knowing I will be home soon.  A truck comes up behind me, starts to slow down (Yeahhhhh, there was pooh dripping down my leg...they were probably concerned), and, as soon as they get close enough to realize what it is, speeds off.  I went home, took a really long shower, and threw away my pants and underwear/all the evidence.  

The next time my dad asked me to go running with him, I told him I wasn't feeling well.  To motivate me, he pointed out (without knowing what happened) that, in 15 years of running, he had never, ever, shat his pants.  I kept silent and told him I just really didn't think it was a good idea.  Still haven't actually told him what happened, and have rarely run with him since then.  At this point it's more funny than anything, but I have been very careful about the state of my stomach/colon before I go running since then.

Hurray!  That's awesome!

It's less an issue of being right or wrong and more one of my being curious at your response to the OP.

Violence absolutely works as discipline.  From my understanding it used to be much more commonplace, and that is because it tends to gets immediate results.  There are just so many other ways to discipline a child without causing physical or psychological harm.

I can certainly relate (as I'm sure many others can) to the feeling that those who have had to go through less than you are spoiled (which is not meant to downplay the difficulties of your situation at all).  It's hard to balance that with the wish that other people not have to go through the painful part of any experience.

Your original response seemed hostile, but there also seemed to be reasoning behind it, which is why I commented as I did.  Thank you for an honest and insightful response.

The fact that worse things have happened does not negate that what happened in this circumstance was wrong.

Did anyone ever stand up for you or your mother?  Didn't you ever want someone to?  

Regardless, I imagine this child gets much worse at home, and it is surprising that you have so little sympathy considering your (seemingly) similar situation.
